A few things to consider. These have been mostly touched on elsewhere in the thread, so my apologies if it's redundant.

First, even though in context your statement is good and valid, "whatever dangers vaccines may someday be proven to have" is a bit of a red herring. I know you aren't arguing from that POV but I think it's worth stating. The vaccinations in question have been broadly administered for decades now, the adverse effects are already well understood.

Second, in terms of parents making the decision, the sentiment typically applied to this notion isn't actually applicable here much same the way it isn't a good idea to let smokers decide not to smoke indoors: It simply affects more than just the person (or child) for whom the decision is made. Additionally, the very parents making these decisions are by and large not medical professionals themselves and are thus unqualified to make them. We now know that when people (read laymen) try to become educated in an effort to make the "right" decision they become confused when they encounter the technical language that is necessary for them to properly understand, and thus default to their original bias (that vaccines are dangerous). While at first this might seem like a disregard for some notion of "parental rights" the above points clearly show this is also not the case.

In conclusion, this isn't' about how to raise your kids, it's about keeping the rest of the population free from disease.

Did you happen to notice that not one comment there took 'the other view'? That would not make it a fair debate. I found serious problems and omissions (examples include saying there were no sources in that article, the 'conspiracy theory' buzzword, assumptions that the money to be made was equal on both sides, failure to discuss any actual science whatsoever throughout, etc etc etc) in every comment there.

First, a good scientific support for vaccines would begin with some demonstrable science -- for example a comparison of vaccinated versus non-vaccinated populations in as similar of circumstances as possible. WHO, Bill Gates, and 'Big Pharma' have the resources to do this, but it still hasn't happened.

Second, the discussion would continue by looking at the injury and death risks of vaccines by things like CVDPCs and the injuries that led to that nearly $3 billion in damage awards (which was entirely ignored on that page) and compare those to the potential health benefits -- the actual potential benefits that is.

Third, other concepts such as a general societal cost-benefit analysis aside from illness and injury, analysis of risks in general and a comparison of these risks to other risks, consideration of the natural order of injuries versus the artificial order -- who gets saved versus who gets burned -- and of course, understandings of personal autonomy with comparative freedoms and restrictions in other risky circumstances.

The Reddit one-sided commenting didn't do any of these things. What you had at Reddit was purely partisan -- and the other side didn't even show up. There will be better debates. They will include "both sides," and those sides won't be purely partisan.
